summary: This work numerically demonstrates Echoed Conditional Displacement (ECD) gates for bosonic control using a fluxonium qubit, achieving vacuum-subspace fidelities exceeding 99.9% and GKP logical fidelities near 99%. The authors develop a semiclassical framework accounting for all-order dispersive terms via displacement transformation, revealing saturation of the dispersive shift $\chi_\mathrm{eff}(|\alpha|^2)$ at large resonator amplitudes and deriving an improved ECD pulse sequence that compensates for photon loss and higher-order nonlinearities.
motivation: Fluxonium qubits operating at half-flux feature suppressed bit-flip relaxation ($T_1 \sim 1$ ms) due to double-well confinement, making them attractive control qubits for ECD gates where qubit bit-flips are the dominant error mechanism. However, the dynamics of strongly driven resonators deviates from standard fourth-order perturbative models, requiring careful treatment of higher-order nonlinearities.
method: The authors numerically simulate a resonator-fluxonium device (Device 1: $g/2\pi = 6.329$ MHz, $\chi/2\pi = 32.77$ kHz, $\kappa/2\pi = 6.37$ kHz, $\omega_q/2\pi = 233$ MHz at half-flux) by solving the full Hamiltonian in a displaced frame. They extract effective dispersive parameters $\Delta_\mathrm{eff}(|\alpha|^2)$ and $\chi_\mathrm{eff}(|\alpha|^2)$ from numerical out-and-back sequences and develop analytical pulse sequences (Eqs. 12a–12c) that explicitly account for photon loss and resonator Kerr nonlinearities.
result: ECD gates targeting $\beta = 2\pi$ displacement achieve vacuum fidelities exceeding 99.9% in ≈600 ns and GKP logical fidelities $\approx 99\%$ in 240 ns with intermediate displacement $|\alpha_0| \approx 20$. The conditional displacement rate $g_\mathrm{CD} = \chi_\mathrm{eff}|\alpha|$ saturates nonmonotonically with $|\alpha|$ due to competing higher-order Kerr terms; photon loss emerges as the primary fidelity-limiting mechanism in the GKP codespace, which the improved ECD sequence mitigates by suppressing residual unconditional displacements by one order of magnitude.
